Video grab taken from the webcam of the mountain guesthouse Kehlsteinhaus, known as the Eagle's Nest, formerly Adolf Hitler's mountain retreat, on early October 24, 2026, after a large fire broke out at the site in the southern German state of Bavaria [AFP]By Caolán Magee and AFPPublished On 24 Oct 202624 Oct 2026
German police have detained a suspect after a fire engulfed the Eagle’s Nest, Adolf Hitler’s notorious Nazi-era mountain retreat in Bavaria, prompting an overnight emergency operation involving about 200 firefighters.
No injuries were reported at the building, known locally as the Kehlsteinhaus. Police said investigators were examining whether a “suspicious person” taken into temporary custody was connected to the blaze.

The fire alarm was triggered by a smoke detector at about 9:50pm (19:50 GMT) on Friday. Emergency crews could see flames rising above the building as they approached and found it “completely ablaze”, according to police.
The retreat’s remote Alpine location, at an altitude of more than 1,800 metres (about 6,000 feet), complicated efforts to extinguish the fire, police spokesperson Lisa Maier said.
While authorities have not announced a cause, German media reported that investigators suspected arson.
The newspaper Bild said emergency responders had encountered a motorcyclist travelling towards them on their way to the scene and that he was subsequently detained. His possible involvement remained under investigation.

“Vinnie will be given all the time he needs. We’re not starting to put together any timeframes.

A gunman in northern France has killed one person and injured five, including a 12-year-old girl who was seriously wounded, in what authorities are calling a racially motivated “terrorist” attack.
The shooting on Friday was carried out as mounting and often violent cost-of-living protests grip the country with more demonstrations expected on Saturday.

So what was behind this attack? And has there been a rise in Islamophobia in Europe?
Here’s what we know:
What has happened in France?
About 10:30am (08:30 GMT) on Friday, a gunman drove through the towns of Trappes and La Verriere, a working class area on the outskirts of Paris with a large immigrant and Muslim population, and fired an automatic weapon randomly at a petrol station, a medical centre and a children’s playground.
The rampage lasted about 15 minutes before the suspect, identified as 39-year-old Kevin T, was arrested. Laurent Mazaury, the local MP, said the suspect told police he wanted to “kill foreigners”. He added: “I think we are facing a racist person.”

France braces for a second wave of protests after worst riots in yearsBy Virginia PietromarchiPublished On 24 Oct 202624 Oct 2026
Paris, France – More than 70,000 police officers and gendarmes are set to be deployed across France as the country braces for a new round of protests against deteriorating school conditions and the rising cost of living.
French authorities have made clear they are determined to prevent Saturday’s demonstrations from descending into the violence that erupted last weekend.
Recommended Stories list of 4 itemslist 1 of 4Macron to meet student groups: Where are France’s protests heading?list 2 of 4France to deploy 70,000 police as country braces for weekend protestslist 3 of 4Are parents in France and Italy liable for damage caused by student protesters?list 4 of 4One person killed in suspected ‘Islamophobic’ shooting near Parisend of list
On October 17, protests that had been largely peaceful were marred by widespread looting, vandalism and clashes, with thousands of businesses damaged or ransacked. More than 2,000 people were taken into police custody, according to official figures.
To prevent a repeat, Interior Minister Laurent Nunez said 20 percent more officers would be deployed than during the previous weekend.
The operation will also involve RAID, an elite police unit usually tasked with counterterrorism and other high-risk interventions. Nunez said its officers would not be directly involved in crowd control but would support other police operations.

Presidential candidates Senator Flavio Bolsonaro and incumbent Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva appear before their debate on October 23, 2026, in Rio de Janeiro, Brazil [Buda Mendes/Getty Images]By Al Jazeera Staff, AFP and APPublished On 24 Oct 202624 Oct 2026
Brazilian President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva and his right-wing rival Flavio Bolsonaro have focused on policy proposals in the final debate before their presidential run-off.
The candidates questioned each other on Friday, two days before the election, about Brazil’s economy, infrastructure and regional development.
Recommended Stories list of 3 itemslist 1 of 3Why social media has become an election issue in Brazil’s presidential racelist 2 of 3Brazil’s Bolsonaro challenges Lula to expand release of personal recordslist 3 of 3What to know as Brazil prepares for tense presidential run-offend of list
Lula challenged his rival’s plan to take a “chainsaw” to public spending in a manner similar to that of Argentina’s libertarian president, Javier Milei.
“I’ll have the same job here [as Milei in Argentina] because you’re leaving the country bankrupt,” Bolsonaro responded.
Bolsonaro, son of former right-wing President Jair Bolsonaro, accused the incumbent of allowing organised crime to expand, driving families into debt and not addressing the higher cost of living.
“He doesn’t know what hunger is,” Brazil’s first working-class president said of Bolsonaro, who responded, “Why are things so expensive?”
Lula questioned the senator’s experience, saying, “He doesn’t know Brazil.”

Israeli soldiers gather at the scene of an earlier fire exchange at a checkpoint near Hebron in the Israeli-occupied West Bank, October 23, 2026 [AFP]By Stephen QuillenPublished On 24 Oct 202624 Oct 2026|Updated: an hour agoUpdated: an hour ago
Israel’s military has launched another major operation in the occupied West Bank, during which it plans to carry out mass arrests, demolish homes and forcibly displace residents.
The operation comes after an attack at an Israeli military checkpoint near Hebron on Friday in which two Israeli soldiers were killed. The two suspected Palestinian gunmen were shot dead.

Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, who ordered a full lockdown of the West Bank, said Israeli forces would go house-to-house in the Hebron neighbourhood that the suspected attackers came from.
“We will act to destroy this place, ⁠to change it completely,” he said.
Israeli rights group B’Tselem warned the Israeli government’s planned offensive amounts to “collective punishment and acts that could constitute war crimes”.
Here’s what we know about the Israeli military operation.
What’s happening in the West Bank?
Israel’s military announced late on Friday that a major “counterterrorism” operation, involving Israeli soldiers, police and other security agents, was under way in the Hebron area of the occupied West Bank.
It said the “targeted” campaign would last “several days”, in addition to operations in “dozens” of other areas across the West Bank.
